newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian court says Rao's commandos like a "shadow".
newsitem.headline: Indian court says Rao's commandos like a "shadow".

text.p: Night and day, former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao and his family are protected by a squad of commandos with black berets and clutching machineguns.
The Supreme Court ruled on Friday that the special protective cover goes with Rao "as the shadow would a man" and cannot be lifted if he appears in court or goes to jail.
The sharp-shooters belong to the Special Protection Group (SPG), formed in 1988 during what parliament then called a period of "wanton killings, arson, looting and other heinous crimes".
The law came four years after Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was shot dead by Sikh bodyguards at the height of a Sikh separatist rebellion in the northern state of Punjab.
The SPG commandos were first assigned to the prime minister and immediate family members.
Indira Gandhi's son, Rajiv, was blown up by a Tamil suicide bomber in May 1991, six months after he quit the premiership.
His assassination, still being investigated, prompted parliament to extend SPG cover to former prime ministers and their families.

The Indian Express newspaper says the SPG currently covers 65 people, including Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, four ex-prime ministers, Rajiv Gandhi's widow, Sonia Gandhi, and senior government officials including some cabinet ministers.
This security budget last year totalled some $10 million for a special commando force of about 3,000 people, the newspaper said.
The SPG became entangled in Rao's tortuous legal proceedings after local court authorities said he would have to abandon his special protection if he appeared in court.
But the Supreme Court ruled on Friday that the "protective cover cannot be lifted from the protectee" and "the protectee is a protectee all the time, as long as he keeps breathing".
Court authorities said the ruling reduced the chances Rao would ever be put in custody in a prison pending trial.
Instead, they said, it was possible he would be held at home, where his SPG cover could operate more freely.
The Supreme Court also ordered two trials involving Rao -- one in a forgery case, the other a criminal cheating case -- shifted from a cramped local court to a more secure location.

Delhi police and the SPG director had argued that "it was almost impossible for them to provide proximate security satisfactorily to Rao when required to be taken to the Tis Hazari Court complex", the court said in its ruling.
Tis Hazari, a run-down maze of 250 courtrooms in teeming central Delhi, has no access control and attracts up to 70,000 visitors and 2,000 cars and scooters each day, the court said.
The security authorities said Rao was "the prime target of Sikh and Kashmiri militant groups", and cited past plans of Tamil and Islamic fundamentalist groups to target Rao.
